case.case_title: Kumaranatunga v. Samarasinghe, Additional Secretary of the Ministry of Defence and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 121/82, decided on 3 February 1983

clause.text: No person shall be arrested except according to law and must be informed of the reason.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the arrest and detention orders under Emergency Regulations and other laws infringed the fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 13(1), 13(2), and 13(4) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the detention orders were ultra vires the Constitution, that he was not informed of the reasons for arrest, and that the arrest and detention amounted to punishment without trial, violating Articles 13(1), (2), and (4).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the detention orders were valid under the Emergency Regulations, that the arrest was justified under the Code of Criminal Procedure Act for a limited period, and that preventive detention is not punishment and thus not prohibited by Article 13(4).
key_facts: Petitioner was arrested on 19 November 1982 under detention order 'A' and detained until 19 January 1983.
Detention orders were made under Regulation 17(1) of Emergency Regulations.
Petitioner was not served with the detention order '1R5' dated 20 November 1982 but was informed of it by a police officer.
The arrest order 'A' referred to past misconduct, not preventive detention.
Emergency Regulations allow restrictions on fundamental rights during a proclaimed emergency.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 13(1) protects against arbitrary arrest and requires arrest according to law with reasons given. However, during a declared emergency, Emergency Regulations can lawfully restrict these rights. Preventive detention is distinct from punishment and is permissible under the Constitution subject to such regulations. Article 13(4) does not apply to preventive detention. The failure to serve the detention order or inform reasons at the time of arrest does not invalidate detention under Emergency Regulations, as reasons can be communicated later through Advisory Committees.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The arrest on 19 November 1982 was justified under the Code of Criminal Procedure for a limited period and was not longer than reasonable. The detention order 'A' was legally defective as it referred to past misconduct, but the arrest and detention were justified under other laws. The detention order '1R5' was valid preventive detention under Regulation 17(1). The petitioner was informed of the new detention order by a police officer, satisfying the requirement to inform reasons. The Emergency Regulations lawfully restricted the fundamental rights under Articles 13(1) and (2).
principles_established: Preventive detention is qualitatively different from punitive detention and is not punishment under Article 13(4).
Emergency Regulations can validly restrict fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 13(1) and (2) during a proclaimed emergency.
Failure to serve a detention order or inform reasons at the time of arrest does not invalidate detention under Emergency Regulations.
Arrest under the Code of Criminal Procedure for a reasonable period is consistent with Article 13(1).
The subjective opinion of the authority making a preventive detention order is not subject to objective judicial review except for mala fides.
precedents_cited: Lowe v. Darling and Sons (1906) 2 K.B. 772
Gopalan v. State of Madras A.I.R. 1950 S.C. 27
Peiris v. Commissioner of Inland Revenue 1963 65 N.L.R. 457
Hazari Mai Kuthiala v. Income Tax Officer
Mohamed Dastagir Sahib v. Third Additional Income Tax Officer 1961 74 L.W. (Madras) 540

Deviprasad Khandelwas & Sons v. Union of India A.I.R. 1969 Bom 163

outcome.holding: The petitioner's application was dismissed. The arrest and detention under the Emergency Regulations were held not to violate Articles 13(1), (2), and (4) of the Constitution. The defective detention order 'A' did not invalidate the arrest and detention. The petitioner was lawfully detained under valid preventive detention orders.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: No costs ordered due to the view on order 'A'.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Articles 13(1), (2), and (4) are central to the court's analysis of the legality of the arrest and detention, defining the constitutional protections against arbitrary arrest and punishment, and the permissible scope of preventive detention under Emergency Regulations.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court analyzed the arrest and detention orders under Articles 13(1), (2), and (4), concluding that preventive detention under Emergency Regulations is not punishment and that the petitioner was lawfully detained despite procedural defects in the initial order.
